1 
 
 
September 3, 2025   
 
 
 
 
    VIA ELECTRONIC SUBMISSION 
 
 
 
Steven L. Lieberman 
Acting Under Secretary for Health 
Department of Veterans Affairs 
810 Vermont Avenue NW 
Washington, DC 20420 
 
Attention: Reproductive Health Services, 38 CFR Part 17 (RIN 2900-AR57) 
 
Dr. Lieberman: 
 
Common Defense is grassroots, veteran-led organization committed to engaging, 
organizing, training, and mobilizing veterans to elevate their voice on the issues that matter 
most to them and to all Americans, including protecting our democracy, fighting for climate 
justice, and promoting a just foreign policy.  We write in formal opposition to the proposed 
rescission of abortion health care and counseling through the U.S. Department of Veterans 
Affairs (VA) health system, on behalf of veterans and military families who would be harmed 
by the loss of these essential reproductive health services.” 
 
VA’s legal justification for this rollback is questionable. The proposal asserts that abortion 
is not “needed” care under 38 U.S.C. §1710, reverting to a decades-old interpretation that no 
abortion is ever necessary for veterans. It leans on a now-outdated 1992 statute that 
excluded abortions from VA care (with extremely limited exceptions) – a provision that was 
arguably superseded by Congress’s 1996 overhaul of VA healthcare authorities. VA 
acknowledged in 2022 that Congress’s intent in 1996 may have been to create a new, 
expansive set of laws for VA care, meaning the old abortion exclusion might no longer 
constrain the agency. Yet VA now takes the most restrictive view of its authority, claiming its 
power to provide abortions is “dubious” or “nonexistent”.  
 
This interpretation is not mandated by any new statute – it is a policy choice to resurrect a 
prior ban. VA cites “decades of Federal policy” (such as the Hyde Amendment’s ban on 
federal abortion funding) as support, but notably Congress has never enacted an explicit 
ban on VA abortion care in the permanent VA healthcare statutes. In fact, when finalizing 
the 2024 rule that allowed limited abortion services, VA found that providing this care was 
necessary to fulfill its duty to “promote, preserve, or restore” veterans’ health. The current 
proposal offers no new data or statutory change to justify overturning that determination – 

2  
 
only a change in Administration policy. We urge VA to recognize that its obligation to veterans’ 
health includes access to abortion in medically dire circumstances, and that nothing in 
federal law compels VA to deprive veterans of this care. 
 
Harmful Impact of Narrow Abortion Exceptions in Practice 
 
VA proposes that veterans will still be protected by a “life of the mother” exception (both 
in VA facilities and under CHAMPVA). The rule’s supplementary information emphasizes 
that VA has “never” understood its policies to bar care for ectopic pregnancies or 
miscarriage complications and notes that no state law outright forbids treating those life-
threatening conditions. The implication is that a strict ban with only a life-of-mother 
exception is sufficient to safeguard patients. This assumption is profoundly contradicted 
by real-world evidence. In states that enacted abortion bans post-Dobbs with similar 
narrow exceptions, pregnant people have been denied or delayed care until their lives were 
in imminent peril. Doctors and hospitals, fearing legal consequences or unclear standards, 
often wait until a patient is at the brink of death or serious injury before providing an 
emergency abortion – a dangerous delay. VA’s proposal disregards extensive 
documentation of how “life-only” exceptions fail patients in practice, leading to 
preventable trauma, infertility, and even death. 
 
Documented cases from abortion-ban states illustrate the grave risks of these 
restrictive policies: 
 
• Delayed Care for Ectopic Pregnancy (Texas): Ectopic pregnancies (implantation 
outside the uterus) are unviable and life-threatening, yet even these have been 
subject to deadly delays. In one Texas case, a 25-year-old woman was turned away 
from a hospital despite signs of an ectopic pregnancy; she returned days later in 
agonizing pain and only obtained treatment after her OB-GYN personally intervened. 
By then the ectopic pregnancy had ruptured – she “nearly bled to death” and required 
emergency surgery, losing a fallopian tube and compromising her future fertility.1 
Another Texas woman endured a similar ordeal at a different hospital and likewise 
lost a fallopian tube and an ovary due to delayed care for an ectopic pregnancy.2 
These cases occurred despite Texas law explicitly allowing treatment of ectopic 
pregnancies, because fear of harsh penalties (including up to life in prison for 
doctors) has created a chilling effect on care.3 VA’s rule would put veterans in the 
same perilous situation – dependent on individual providers’ willingness to risk legal 
uncertainty while a patient’s condition deteriorates. 
 
1 Tuma, M. (2024, August 13).  Texas women denied abortions for ectopic pregnancies demand federal 
investigation. The Guardian. https://www.theguardian.com/world/article/2024/aug/13/texas-abortion-
ectopic-pregnancy-investigation  
2 Ibid 
3 Salhotra, P. (2024, November 3). Texas Tribune. https://www.texastribune.org/2024/11/03/texas-ob-gyn-
letter-abortion-laws  

3  
 
 
• Forced to Septic Shock after Water Breaks (Texas): In Zurawski v. Texas case, five 
women sued after being denied medically indicated abortions under Texas’s ban.4 
Lead plaintiff Amanda Zurawski’s water broke at 18 weeks (pre-viability), threatening 
infection, but doctors refused to intervene as long as the fetal heartbeat was 
detectable. She was sent home until she developed a life-threatening infection, and 
by the time the hospital “finally agreed she was sick enough” to induce labor, 
Zurawski was septic and spent three days in the ICU. She survived, but the delay 
caused scar tissue that permanently closed one of her fallopian tubes, rendering her 
unable to conceive naturally. This preventable outcome – nearly dying and losing 
fertility – occurred under a life-of-the-mother only exception. It underscores that 
requiring physicians to wait until a patient is at imminent risk of death is 
medically dangerous. Had care been provided when her membranes ruptured 
(before infection set in), her life and fertility would have been better protected. 
Veterans should not suffer under a policy that seeks to duplicate this nightmare. 
• Miscarriage Denied Care Until Emergency (Louisiana): In Louisiana, where 
abortion is banned with only narrow exceptions, a pregnant woman experiencing an 
early miscarriage was denied proper treatment because the fetus still had faint 
cardiac activity.5 She arrived at an ER with severe pain and bleeding, and tests showed 
the pregnancy was no longer viable (the fetus had stopped growing, with abnormally 
low hormone levels). Yet hospital staff refused to confirm she was miscarrying or offer 
a standard uterine evacuation (dilation & curettage or medication) while any 
heartbeat remained. They sent her home to “wait,” despite the increased risk of 
hemorrhage or infection the longer a failed pregnancy is left untreated. When her 
condition worsened to an emergency (soaking through her clothes with blood, labor-
like pain), a second hospital still hesitated – a doctor there would not even document 
“spontaneous abortion” in her file due to fear of legal “investigation”. The patient and 
her husband were left terrified and traumatized; they have since put off plans to have 
another child. This incident is emblematic of how vague exceptions force pregnant 
people to endure needless suffering and danger until a situation qualifies as a clear 
“medical emergency.” VA’s proposal, by eliminating abortion counseling and care 
even for serious health indications, would import these same perils into federal 
veteran care. 
 
VA’s confidence that “the lives of pregnant women will continue to be protected” without the 
2022 rule rings hollow in light of these stories and obscures the plain reality that a “life 
endangerment only” rule is unworkable and cruel. Physicians often cannot pinpoint the 
exact moment when a patient crosses from mere risk to certain death. Fear of prosecution 
 
4 Kawaja, C. (2024, June 27). Zurawski V. Texas: Abortion Exceptions As The New Legal Battleground For 
Women’s Lives. Health Affairs. https://www.healthaffairs.org/content/forefront/zurawski-v-texas-abortion-
exceptions-new-legal-battleground-women-s-lives  
5 Westwood, R. (2022, December 29). Bleeding and in pain, she couldn’t get 2 Louisiana ERs to answer: Is it a 
miscarriage? NPR. https://www.npr.org/sections/health-shots/2022/12/29/1143823727/bleeding-and-in-
pain-she-couldnt-get-2-louisiana-ers-to-answer-is-it-a-miscarria  

4  
 
leads hospitals to err on the side of not treating until a patient’s condition is critical. In fact, 
states with bans have seen avoidable harms proliferate: researchers have documented that 
many exceptions are so ill-defined that hospital lawyers must be consulted while patients 
suffer, and care is often withheld until a patient’s “health deteriorates” dangerously.6  
 
Even some conditions that do threaten long-term health or fertility (for example, severe 
hypertension, or incomplete miscarriages) have not been deemed sufficient under strict 
bans.7 By stripping away the rape, incest, and health exceptions in VA policy, the rule virtually 
guarantees similar tragedies among veterans and their families. It would impose one of the 
most extreme abortion restrictions in the country on those who rely on VA care – even in 
states where abortion remains legal. This is an abdication of VA’s duty to provide evidence-
based, patient-centered care for those who served. 
 
CHAMPVA vs. TRICARE: Inconsistent Standards and “Similar” 
Benefits 
 
The proposed rule also affects CHAMPVA, the VA-run health coverage for certain veteran 
dependents and survivors. VA contends that CHAMPVA is only required to provide 
benefits “similar” – not identical – to the Department of Defense’s (DOD’s) TRICARE 
insurance. VA’s longstanding regulation (38 C.F.R. §17.270(b)) indeed authorizes 
CHAMPVA to cover medically necessary services unless specifically excluded, paralleling 
TRICARE’s model. The statute establishing CHAMPVA (38 U.S.C. §1781) says care shall be 
provided “in the same or similar manner and subject to the same or similar limitations” as 
care in the DoD system.  
 
Under current DoD/TRICARE policy, military families are covered for abortion if a 
pregnancy is the result of rape or incest or poses a risk to the mother’s life.8 TRICARE also 
explicitly covers the medically necessary treatment of ectopic pregnancies and 
miscarriages as distinct from elective abortion. Prior to 2022, CHAMPVA’s regulations were 
actually more restrictive than TRICARE’s – CHAMPVA only paid for abortions if continuing 
the pregnancy would endanger the mother’s life, excluding cases of rape or incest. The 2022 
interim final rule brought CHAMPVA in line with TRICARE’s standard (and slightly beyond, by 
including serious health endangerment). The new proposal would restore the old disparity: 
CHAMPVA would once again exclude coverage for rape or incest pregnancies, covering 
abortion only to save the mother’s life. This creates an unjust inconsistency between two 
classes of federal beneficiaries. For example, an active-duty servicemember’s wife 
impregnated by rape can have a TRICARE-covered abortion, but a veteran’s wife in the same 
 
6 Felx M, Sobel L, & Salganicoff A. (2024, June 6). A Review of Exceptions in State Abortion Bans: Implications 
for the Provision of Abortion Services. KFF. https://www.kff.org/womens-health-policy/a-review-of-
exceptions-in-state-abortions-bans-implications-for-the-provision-of-abortion-services/  
7 Ibid. 
8 Humana Military (TRICARE contractor). TRICARE Abortion Coverage Guidelines (2023). 
https://www.humanamilitary.com/provider/resources/abortion  

5  
 
horrific situation under CHAMPVA would have no coverage and no VA facility care under this 
rule. VA offers no compelling reasoning for denying veteran families a protection that 
Congress ensured for military families. 
 
While VA is correct that it can deviate from TRICARE in designing CHAMPVA’s benefits, such 
deviations should be grounded in the needs of the population and medical necessity – 
not torn asunder by ideological currents and partisan agendas. Common Defense 
believes the intended spirit of 38 U.S.C. §1781 was to ensure that families of veterans 
receive comparable care to families of active servicemembers. Reverting to a policy where 
CHAMPVA excludes rape and incest cases (when TRICARE covers them) undermines that 
principle of equity. It certainly does not “promote the health” of veterans’ loved ones. VA 
cites no evidence that offering coverage for these rare, tragic circumstances was harmful or 
unnecessary. On the contrary, providing those exceptions in CHAMPVA since 2022 has 
aligned VA’s practice with basic federal standards and avoided cruel outcomes.  
 
We urge VA to consider that “similar” should mean comparable in scope and fairness. If 
anything, VA should be arguing to maintain or expand coverage, since TRICARE’s limitations 
themselves stem from external statutory restrictions (10 U.S.C. §1093) rather than optimal 
healthcare policy. Instead, VA proposes to strictly copy the most restrictive interpretation – 
and even goes further by prohibiting “abortion counseling” outright in CHAMPVA. By 
contrast, TRICARE’s rules do not bar physicians from discussing or advising patients about 
abortion options; they simply state that abortion counseling is not reimbursed as a separate 
covered service unless medically necessary. That is a billing limitation, not a gag on medical 
communication. VA’s approach is far more extreme, effectively chilling doctor-patient 
communication and undermining informed consent in a way that TRICARE does not. 
 
VA’s proposal to forbid even counseling goes beyond merely aligning with DoD; it 
weaponizes VA benefits package to silence healthcare professionals from advising 
veterans and families of all their medical options. This is a disservice to beneficiaries and 
inconsistent with standard medical practice. 
 
In sum, the “similar, not identical” clause should not be a license to provide inferior 
coverage. VA has previously upheld that this clause empowers it to do the right thing for 
CHAMPVA families. To now use the clause to strip away vital benefits is arbitrary and 
capricious. It ignores the moral and practical stakes: CHAMPVA beneficiaries losing 
coverage for rape or incest-related care will face the same hardships as veterans 
themselves – potentially traveling hundreds of miles or paying out of pocket to find safe care, 
or worse, being forced to continue traumatizing or dangerous pregnancies. VA provides no 
data that this change “ensures needed services” as claimed; it simply declares, ipse dixit, 
that abortion is not “medically necessary and appropriate” for CHAMPVA patients. This 
conclusion is unsupported by medical consensus and appears driven by ideology rather 
than VA’s healthcare mandate. 
 

6  
 
Gaps in VAs Justification and Data 
 
VA’s notice repeatedly asserts that abortions are not “needed” care for veterans, but it fails 
to engage with the evidence to the contrary. In 2022, VA conducted a thorough and 
reasoned analysis of veterans’ healthcare needs in light of the Dobbs decision. The resulting 
interim final rule explicitly recognized that state bans posed urgent risks to the lives and 
health of pregnant veterans, and concluded that abortion access—under circumstances of 
rape, incest, or serious medical threat—was needed care and consistent with VA’s mission 
to protect veteran health.9 
 
The rulemaking docket at that time documented veterans’ unique risk factors: women 
veterans (the fastest-growing segment of VA patients) have higher rates of chronic health 
conditions (like severe hypertension and diabetes) that can make pregnancy extremely 
dangerous. Many veterans also suffer from service-connected mental health conditions or 
trauma: for example, one in three women veterans report having experienced military sexual 
assault or trauma (MST) during their service. As VA acknowledged in 2022, pregnancy can 
exacerbate PTSD and other mental health conditions, and in some cases an abortion may 
be necessary to preserve a veteran’s life or health (for instance, risk of suicide or other grave 
harm). The prior administration’s rule recognized that in the aftermath of Dobbs, veterans 
in states banning abortion would be left in crisis – especially those dealing with MST-
related pregnancies or serious medical complications. By ignoring these findings, the new 
proposal fails the test of reasoned decision-making. VA offers no medical rebuttal to the 
proposition that abortions are needed to save a woman’s life or health. Instead, it relies on 
a stale assertion that for “nearly fifty years” federal policy refused to fund “elective” 
abortions. 
 
VA’s careless haste is most evident in this portion of the rule’s justification. The services at 
issue here (cases of rape, incest, lethal fetal anomalies, emergency health risks) are not 
elective – they are medically indicated and often time-sensitive. VA’s conflation of all 
abortion care with “elective” procedures is a mischaracterization that evades the real 
question: Will veterans suffer or die without this care? All available evidence says yes, they 
will – as the examples above demonstrate. 
 
VA also emphasizes that it has provided very few abortions since the 2022 policy change, 
suggesting that the “high demand” anticipated “never materialized”. These statistics are not 
the vindication the Department thinks it is. 
 
If “only” 40 CHAMPVA beneficiaries and a similar number of veterans obtained abortions 
per year, those cases represent real people whose lives or well-being were safeguarded 
by VA health care. The small number is not evidence of a lack of need – it is evidence that 
 
9 Department of Veterans Affairs, Interim Final Rule: Reproductive Health Services, 87 Fed. Reg. 55287 (2022, 
September 9) https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2022/09/09/2022-19239/reproductive-health-
services  

7  
 
VA’s limited exceptions were working as a safety net for the most acute situations with 
minimal impact to operational bandwidth. Those are precisely the cases where government 
support matters most. The fact that hundreds of veterans did not flood VA hospitals for 
abortions does not mean the policy was purposeless; it means veterans use VA abortion 
services only as a last resort when faced with dire circumstances, as intended.  
 
Further, VA provides no data showing any negative outcomes or misuse of the policy – no 
spike in “elective” abortions on demand, no strain on resources. In the absence of such 
evidence, revoking a lifesaving benefit from a small, vulnerable subset of patients is 
arbitrary and unjustified. 
 
It is also noteworthy that VA’s proposal touts consistency with “decades of past practice” 
yet fails to grapple with the radically changed post-Roe landscape. This landscape is not 
an abstract hypothetical; it is grounded in maternal health crises that are ongoing and well-
documented. Prior to 2022, veterans always had the legal option to seek abortion care 
outside the VA if needed (since Roe v. Wade protected that right nationally). VA’s pre-2022 
stance existed in a context where, theoretically, a veteran in Texas or Alabama could visit a 
local clinic. After Dobbs, that is no longer true in at least 12 states with total bans.10 Many 
veterans in those states now face exactly the scenario the 2022 rule was meant to prevent: 
they must either travel hundreds of miles to a state where abortion is legal, pay significant 
out-of-pocket costs, or carry a high-risk or nonviable pregnancy to term.  
 
VA’s own 2022 Regulatory Impact Analysis projected significant need for abortion services—
estimating that over 1,000 veterans and CHAMPVA beneficiaries might rely on the expanded 
policy each year. In practice, far fewer cases were reported. The current proposal seizes on 
that disparity to suggest that veterans do not truly need abortion services. But that 
conclusion ignores a more plausible explanation: many veterans and CHAMPVA 
beneficiaries may not have even been aware that these services were available, and those 
who were often faced barriers such as travel distance, cost, stigma, or logistical delays in 
seeking care outside VA facilities. Yet the proposal provides no meaningful economic or 
public health analysis of these burdens. By omitting any discussion of how eliminating 
abortion access will affect veterans’ health outcomes, costs, or safety, VA fails to meet its 
obligation to assess the real-world consequences of its rule. There is no estimate of the 
likely increase in medical complications, mental health crises, or maternal mortality that 
could result from eliminating abortion access at VA. Such an omission is glaring, given that 
maternal morbidity has already measurably risen in states that have restricted abortion 
access. 
 
By neglecting to address these outcomes, VA fails to meet its obligation under the 
Administrative Procedure Act to examine the relevant data and effects of its rule. This 
silence on veteran health outcomes is a gap in the record that cannot be overlooked. 
 
10 (2025, August 6). Fact Sheet: Abortion Access for Veterans. Center for Reproductive Rights.  
https://reproductiverights.org/fact-sheet-abortion-access-veterans/  

8  
 
 
Public Opinion and Common Defense Petition 
 
This proposed rule has generated a groundswell of public opposition, including from 
veterans, medical experts, and lawmakers. A bipartisan group of Members of Congress has 
already written to VA urging that the current abortion access policy be maintained, stressing 
that “without this rule, pregnant veterans in states that ban abortion would have been 
denied access to needed care at VA” and forced to seek “urgently needed healthcare” far 
from home.11  
 
Common Defense’s membership has also spoken out. We provided a petition to our 
membership in opposition to the rule, which has since received 5,273 signatories from 
veterans and military family members across the country. Veterans and their families do not 
want to see the Department of Veterans Affairs turned into a battleground for culture wars 
at the expense of patients’ lives. They expect their VA to offer comprehensive, veterans first 
healthcare, not to impose additional hardships. 
 
Moreover, leading medical organizations have emphasized that abortion, including 
counseling, is a standard and sometimes medically necessary part of healthcare. By 
banning “abortion counseling” even in situations where a veteran is pregnant and ill, VA 
would be gagging its clinicians from providing honest medical advice. This runs contrary to 
medical ethics and informed consent principles. In VA’s own system, many patients have 
complex health profiles (due to age, disabilities, or war-related conditions) that make 
pregnancy especially high-risk. These patients merit full information about their options – 
possibly more so than the average patient – yet the proposed rule would silence VA doctors 
and nurses from even discussing abortion as an option. Such a policy goes beyond any 
federal requirement (even Title X “gag rules” were rescinded in civilian clinics) and will foster 
confusion and mistrust. It is notable that during the short period VA has allowed abortion 
counseling and referrals (since 2022), there is no evidence of abuse or misconduct. If 
anything, it has allowed VA to coordinate care for veterans who needed to go outside the 
system. The elimination of counseling serves no rational purpose except to further 
ideologically stigmatize abortion and deter patients from seeking help. This is antithetical to 
the VA’s patient-centered mission. 
 
Conclusion: Preserve Needed Care for Veterans and Families 
 
We urge the Department of Veterans Affairs to withdraw or substantially revise this 
proposed rule. The blanket exclusion of abortion services and counseling would endanger 
veterans’ lives, undermine their autonomy, and break faith with the promise of care we owe 
to those who served. VA’s own justification is legally and factually flawed – it ignores clear

9  
 
evidence of harm under restrictive laws, contradicts Congress’s intent to provide 
comparable care to veteran families (CHAMPVA vs. TRICARE), and fails to offer any data-
driven rationale for why the 2022 policy expansion should be reversed. As a federal agency, 
VA is bound by the requirements of the Administrative Procedure Act to base its regulations 
on evidence and to articulate a reasoned explanation. Here, the explanation is lacking, and 
the costs to veterans’ health are unaccounted for. 
 
Veterans have put their lives on the line for this country; they deserve a VA that will fight just 
as hard for their health and well-being. The 5,273 veterans and family members who signed 
the Common Defense petition, along with major veteran service organizations and medical 
professionals, have made their message clear: do not take away abortion care and 
counseling from those who need it. VA should maintain the current policy that provides 
limited, necessary abortion services (in cases of rape, incest, or danger to life/health) and 
related counseling. If improvements are needed, it should be toward expanding support – 
for example, ensuring every VA facility is prepared to handle emergency obstetric care and 
that veterans are aware of their benefits – not toward stripping away care. We call on the 
Department of Veterans Affairs to put aside political pressure and uphold its sacred 
obligation to care for veterans and their families, which includes safeguarding their 
reproductive health and lives. 
 
This comment is submitted on behalf of Common Defense and the 5,273 undersigned 
individuals who have joined us in urging the Department of Veterans Affairs to withdraw 
this harmful proposed rule.
